Title: Known issues when using Quarkus >= 3.31 with Mandrel 23.1 for JDK 21 · Issue #52316 · quarkusio/quarkus
URL: https://github.com/quarkusio/quarkus/issues/52316
Published: 2026-02-02T12:30:56.000Z
Author: zakkak
Highlights:
## Known issues when using Quarkus >= 3.31 with Mandrel 23.1 for JDK 21

- Author: [@zakkak](https://github.com/zakkak)
- Association: MEMBER
- State: open
- Labels: area/native-image
- Created: 2026-02-02T12:30:56Z
- Updated: 2026-02-03T10:39:44Z

Starting with Quarkus 3.31 the default builder image is Mandrel 25.0.
The goal of this tracker is to gather all known issues that may arise when using Mandrel 23.1 for JDK 21 with Quarkus >= 3.31.

## Thread dumps

Quarkus historically came with its own thread dumper, being registered as a `SIGQUIT` handler.

Starting with Mandrel 24.2 for JDK 24, JCMD became available which also relies on a `SIGQUIT` handler. As a result, Quarkus drops its legacy thread dumper in favor of JCMD and GraalVM/Mandrel's native thread dumper when using Mandrel >= 24.2.

Since the thread dumper implementation is decided based on the current Mandrel version this is not expected to cause any issues (other than getting differently formatted dumps) when the Mandrel version is known. 
However, Quarkus supports [separating java and native-image compilation](https://quarkus.io/version/main/guides/building-native-image#separating-java-and-native-image-compilation) which results in Quarkus configuring itself for the default Mandrel version (25 for Quarkus >= 3.31) instead of the one that will eventually compile the code to a native executable.

As a result, if one tries to build a Quarkus application using `-Dquarkus.native.sources-only=true` and then using Mandrel 23.1, the build fails with:

```
Error: The '--enable-monitoring' option contains invalid value(s): threaddump. It can only contain 'heapdump', 'jfr', 'jvmstat', 'jmxserver' (experimental), 'jmxclient' (experimental), or 'all' (deprecated behavior: defaults to 'all' if no argument is provided).
Internal exception: com.oracle.svm.core.util.UserError$UserException: The '--enable-monitoring' option contains invalid value(s): threaddump. It can only contain 'heapdump', 'jfr', 'jvmstat', 'jmxserver' (experimental), 'jmxclient' (experimental), or 'all' (deprecated behavior: defaults to 'all' if no argument is provided).
```

To work around this issue please edit `target/native-sources/native-image.args` before invoking Mandrel and remove `threaddump` from the `--enable-monitoring=` option.

Title: Reachability Metadata
URL: https://www.graalvm.org/jdk25/reference-manual/native-image/metadata/
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
The dynamic language features of the JVM (for example, reflection and resource handling) compute the dynamically-accessed program elements such as fields, methods, or resource URLs at run time. On HotSpot this is possible because all class files and resources are available at run time and can be loaded by the runtime. Availability of all classes and resources, and their loading at run time, comes with an extra overhead in memory and startup time.

To make native binaries small, the `native-image` builder performs static analysis at build time to determine only the necessary program elements that are needed for the correctness of the application. Small binaries allow fast application startup and low memory footprint, however they come at a cost: determining dynamically-accessed application elements via static analysis is infeasible as reachability of those elements depends on data that is available only at run time.

To ensure inclusion of necessary dynamically-accessed elements into the native binary, the `native-image` builder requires reachability metadata (hereinafter referred to as metadata). Providing the builder with correct and exhaustive reachability metadata guarantees application correctness and ensures compatibility with third-party libraries at runtime.

You can provide reachability metadata to the `native-image` builder using the following methods:

- Compute metadata in code when the native binary is built and store the required elements in the initial heap of the native binary.
- Place one or more reachability-metadata.json files in the META-INF/native-image/ / / directory on the classpath. For more information about how to collect metadata for your application automatically, see Collecting Metadata Automatically.
- Use the `-H:Preserve= ` flag. For detailed instructions, please refer to the `-H:Preserve=` documentation.
- Use the Feature API for advanced use cases where classpath scanning is necessary to compute correct metadata.

> Note: Native Image is migrating to the more user-friendly implementation of reachability metadata that shows problems early on and allows easy debugging.
> 
> To enable the new user-friendly reachability-metadata mode for your application, pass the option `--exact-reachability-metadata` at build time. To enable the user-friendly mode only for concrete packages, pass `--exact-reachability-metadata= `.
> 
> To get an overview of all places in your code where missing registrations occur, without committing to the exact behavior, you can pass `-XX:MissingRegistrationReportingMode=Warn` when starting the application.
> 
> To detect places where the application accidentally ignores a missing registration error (with `catch (Throwable t)` blocks), pass `-XX:MissingRegistrationReportingMode=Exit` when starting the application. The application will then unconditionally print the error message with the stack trace and exit immediately. This behavior is ideal for running application tests to guarantee all metadata is included.

# URL Protocols in Native Image

Native Image includes URL protocol handlers that are reachable in the generated binary. The `file` and `resource` URL protocols are enabled by default. Resources must still be included through reachability metadata before the `resource` protocol can resolve them.

Other JDK URL protocol handlers are supported but not enabled by default. To use one, register the corresponding `sun.net.www.protocol..Handler` constructor in reachability metadata. For example, to use the `http` and `https` protocols, add this entry to META-INF/native-image/reachability-metadata.json:

```json
{
  "reflection": [
    {
      "type": "sun.net.www.protocol.http.Handler",
      "methods": [
        {
          "name": "<init>",
          "parameterTypes": []
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "type": "sun.net.www.protocol.https.Handler",
      "methods": [
        {
          "name": "<init>",
          "parameterTypes": []
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

```

Use the same form for other JDK protocols, for example `jar`, `jrt`, `ftp`, `jmod`, or `mailto`, by replacing the protocol name in the handler class. For `jrt`, registering `sun.net.www.protocol.jrt.Handler` only enables URL construction. Opening a `jrt:` connection also requires `-H:+AllowJRTFileSystem`, and runtime module access depends on `java.home`. If a native executable accesses a supported protocol that was not registered, the URL lookup fails at run time and reports the handler class that must be added to reachability metadata.

The `--enable-http`, `--enable-https`, and `--enable-url-protocols` options are deprecated. Use reachability metadata instead.

# public Interface WebSocket

---

A WebSocket Client.

`WebSocket` instances are created through WebSocket.Builder.

WebSocket has an input and an output side. These sides are independent from each other. A side can either be open or closed. Once closed, the side remains closed. WebSocket messages are sent through a`WebSocket` and received through a`WebSocket.Listener` associated with it. Messages can be sent until the WebSocket's output is closed, and received until the WebSocket's input is closed.

A send method is any of the`sendText`,`sendBinary`,`sendPing`,`sendPong` and`sendClose` methods of`WebSocket`. A send method initiates a send operation and returns a`CompletableFuture` which completes once the operation has completed. If the`CompletableFuture` completes normally the operation is considered succeeded. If the`CompletableFuture` completes exceptionally, the operation is considered failed. An operation that has been initiated but not yet completed is considered pending.

A receive method is any of the`onText`,`onBinary`,`onPing`,`onPong` and`onClose` methods of`Listener`. WebSocket initiates a receive operation by invoking a receive method on the listener. The listener then must return a`CompletionStage` which completes once the operation has completed.

To control receiving of messages, a WebSocket maintains an internal counter. This counter's value is a number of times the WebSocket has yet to invoke a receive method. While this counter is zero the WebSocket does not invoke receive methods. The counter is incremented by`n` when`request(n)` is called. The counter is decremented by one when the WebSocket invokes a receive method.`onOpen` and`onError` are not receive methods. WebSocket invokes`onOpen` prior to any other methods on the listener. WebSocket invokes`onOpen` at most once. WebSocket may invoke`onError` at any given time. If the WebSocket invokes`onError` or`onClose`, then no further listener's methods will be invoked, no matter the value of the counter. For a newly built WebSocket the counter is zero.

...

`WebSocket` handles received Ping and Close messages automatically (as per the WebSocket Protocol) by replying with Pong and Close messages. If the listener receives Ping or Close messages, no mandatory actions from the listener are required.

You do **not** need GraalVM installed locally if the Dockerfile builds with a Quarkus Mandrel builder image. You **do** need:

- Docker (BuildKit) or Podman, with roughly **6–8 GB RAM** available for `native-image`
- A **Maven wrapper** in `lib/java` (the Mandrel builder image does not ship Maven)
- To switch the Dockerfile from the current JVM build to a **Mandrel/GraalVM builder + micro runtime** image
- Quarkus 3.39.1 requires **GraalVM/Mandrel 25+**, so use the `jdk-25` builder image — not `jdk-21`

The current Dockerfile is JVM-only (`maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17` → `eclipse-temurin:17-jre`). Native requires replacing both stages.

## Plan

### 1. Add a Maven wrapper to `lib/java`

The Quarkus builder image contains Mandrel + `native-image`, but not Maven. Add:

- `lib/java/mvnw`
- `lib/java/.mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties`

Then the Docker build can run `./mvnw` inside the builder image. (`lib/java` is already copied by the Dockerfile.)

### 2. Add a `native` profile to `lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/pom.xml`

Quarkus' standard native profile:

```xml
<profiles>
  <profile>
    <id>native</id>
    <activation>
      <property><name>native</name></property>
    </activation>
    <properties>
      <quarkus.native.enabled>true</quarkus.native.enabled>
      <quarkus.package.jar.enabled>false</quarkus.package.jar.enabled>
    </properties>
  </profile>
</profiles>
```

### 3. Add native resource configuration

Most demo resources are already under `META-INF/resources`, which Quarkus includes automatically in native images. The base CSS is not, so add to `lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/src/main/resources/application.properties`:

```properties
quarkus.native.resources.includes=dev/pathland/render/html/base.css,dev/pathland/render/html/base.css.name
```

This covers `BaseCss` if it is initialized at runtime. The DOM bundle, service worker, icons, lyrics, and 22 MB of audio/cover assets are already under `META-INF/resources` and should be included automatically.

### 4. Replace the Dockerfile stages

Stage 1 — build with Mandrel 25:

```dockerfile
FROM quay.io/quarkus/ubi9-quarkus-mandrel-builder-image:jdk-25 AS build

USER root
WORKDIR /src
COPY lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html/assets ./lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html/assets
COPY --chown=quarkus:quarkus lib/java ./lib/java
RUN chmod +x lib/java/mvnw

USER quarkus
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/home/quarkus/.m2 \
    cd lib/java && ./mvnw -q -B \
      -pl pathland-quarkus-demo,pathland-quarkus-deployment -am \
      package -Dnative -Dmaven.test.skip=true \
      -Dquarkus.native.native-image-xmx=4g
```

Stage 2 — minimal runtime:

```dockerfile
FROM quay.io/quarkus/ubi9-quarkus-micro-image:2.0

WORKDIR /work/
COPY --from=build /src/lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/target/*-runner /work/application
RUN chmod 775 /work /work/application \
    && chown -R 1001 /work \
    && chmod -R "g+rwX" /work \
    && chown -R 1001:root /work

EXPOSE 8080
ENV QUARKUS_HTTP_PORT=8080
USER 1001
ENTRYPOINT ["./application", "-Dquarkus.http.host=0.0.0.0"]
```

Notes:
- `jdk-25` is required by Quarkus 3.39.1 (minimum GraalVM/Mandrel 25).
- If you specifically want GraalVM CE instead of Mandrel, use `quay.io/quarkus/ubi9-quarkus-graalvmce-builder-image:jdk-25`.
- On Apple Silicon, build with `--platform linux/amd64` if deploying to Render/x86_64; otherwise Docker builds a linux/arm64 binary.

### 5. Likely follow-ups if the first native build/runtime fails

These are the only non-obvious risks:

- **JDK WebSocket proxy** (`/ad` uses `java.net.http.WebSocket`): verify the proxied ad app works in native. If not, add:
  ```properties
  quarkus.native.additional-build-args=--initialize-at-run-time=java.net.http,jdk.internal.net.http
  ```
  or switch the Quarkus starter's `ProxyTransport` to a Quarkus WebSockets Next client.
- **JNA**: `pathland-view-core` carries JNA for desktop interop, but the server path does not use it. If the native build complains, either exclude `jna` from the demo's runtime dependencies or add `--initialize-at-run-time=com.sun.jna`.
- **Redis state serialization**: the demo defaults to in-memory state. If you run it with `REDIS_URL`, native Java serialization of state values needs reachability metadata; the default demo path does not.

### 6. Verify

Build and run:

```bash
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64 \
  -f lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/Dockerfile \
  -t pathland-quarkus-demo:native .

docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 pathland-quarkus-demo:native
```

Check:

- `GET /` returns hydrated SSR HTML
- `GET /ad` and `GET /kotlin`
- WebSocket upgrade at `/_pathland/ws` and `/ad/_pathland/ws`
- `GET /_pathland/assets/audio/track1.mp3` (Range/seek)
- `GET /_pathland/base-<hash>.css`
- `GET /_pathland/sw.js` headers
- `GET /q/health` and `GET /q/metrics`
- The `/ad` proxy inside the player (the native WebSocket risk)
- Startup time and memory (should be far below the current 256 MB JVM cap)

### 7. Update docs

`docs/DEPLOY.md` currently says “JRE 17 runtime, no native build”. Update it to document:

- Mandrel 25 builder requirement
- Maven wrapper
- `--platform linux/amd64` for Render
- Native image build time/memory
- The Redis serialization caveat

Optionally add a native build job to CI, but that is slow and can be a separate workflow.

## Decisions to confirm

1. Replace the existing `Dockerfile` with the native one, or add a separate `Dockerfile.native` and keep the JVM image?
2. Mandrel (recommended for Quarkus) or GraalVM CE?
3. OK to add the Maven wrapper under `lib/java`?
4. Is the target Render/x86_64, or do you also need arm64/multi-arch?

- Move base.css to resources perhaps?

parts.text:
Key findings:
- Only two ffm files: PathlandCore.kt, RingOpcodeSink.kt.
- Only references outside view-core are in `pathland-desktop-demo` (GtkHost, GtkRendererNative, QtHost, QtRendererNative) and docs/status. Also `RingOpcodeSink` referenced in desktop status. No server/HTML/DSL references.
- `RingOpcodeSink` depends on `dev.pathland.view.core.protocol.*` and `transport.OpcodeSink` and `AttributedString`, `TokenPath`, `ValueEncoder`. So the new module depends on `pathland-view-core`.
- `PathlandCore` depends on `dev.pathland.view.core.protocol.Opcode`.
- JNA dependency is only in `pathland-view-core/pom.xml` and `pathland-desktop-demo/pom.xml`.
- `pathland-view-core` tests don't reference ffm (only FrameOpcodeSink). So moving ffm out won't affect view-core tests.
- The `pathland-desktop-demo` already has JNA dependency directly, but it imports ffm from view-core. After moving, it needs dependency on `pathland-native-core` (new module).
- Root `lib/java/pom.xml` modules: libraries (pathland-view-core, pathland-render-html, pathland-server-core, spring starter, quarkus, quarkus-deployment) + demos profile (demo-views-kotlin, desktop-demo, quarkus-demo, spring-demo). Where should `pathland-native-core` go? It's a library (JNA ring interop) used by desktop demo. If it's publishable, add to base modules and dependencyManagement. If it's only for demos, add to `demos` profile. But the user suggests `pathland-native-core` as a module; likely a library. It could be published for desktop hosts. However, it depends on `pathland-view-core`; both are libraries. Add to base modules so it's built/tested and published. But it requires JNA, which is fine for a library. The whole point is that server consumers (pathland-view-core) don't pull JNA. The new module is opt-in.
- Need to consider the Maven Central release profile and Dokka/javadoc. `pathland-view-core` is Kotlin-first and has a Dokka profile for javadoc. The new module is Kotlin-only; for `-P release`, it needs a javadoc jar. The parent `lib/java/pom.xml` release profile attaches sources + javadoc for all modules. For Kotlin-only module, JDK javadoc fails (same as view-core). We need to copy the Dokka profile into the new module or configure `maven.javadoc.skip` + Dokka. Let's inspect the parent release profile to see how javadoc is configured and whether view-core's profile is the only special case. We saw view-core has a `release` profile with `maven.javadoc.skip=true` and Dokka. The new module needs the same. Also `pathland-server-core` is Kotlin+Java and uses JDK javadoc? It has Java sources and Kotlin tests; maybe javadoc works because main is Java. The new module is Kotlin-only, so needs Dokka.
- Alternatively, make `pathland-native-core` a demo-only module (not published), avoiding release/javadoc concerns. But the user might want it as a reusable library. Ask? The name suggests library. We can propose adding it as a published library with the same Dokka release profile as view-core. Or, to minimize scope, add it to the `demos` profile because only the desktop demo uses it. But "native core" is likely intended for native hosts, so publishable. Let's present the tradeoff and recommend publishing it as a library (consistent with the "reusable JVM library set") but note it needs Dokka.

- Also `pathland-view-core/status.md` must be updated to remove JNA interop and note it moved to `pathland-native-core/status.md`. `pathland-desktop-demo/status.md` update imports. AGENTS.md update (architecture, module list, status). `lib/java/pom.xml` description and JNA comment. `docs/NLNET-APPLICATION.md` maybe not necessary. `docs/GRANT.md` mentions JNA; fine.

- The new module's package: Should it keep `dev.pathland.view.core.ffm` or move to `dev.pathland.nativecore`? If we move to a new artifact but keep the package, it's source-compatible for consumers (desktop demo imports remain the same) and only the dependency changes. That's less churn. But the module name `pathland-native-core` with package `dev.pathland.view.core.ffm` is slightly inconsistent. We could rename package to `dev.pathland.nativecore` (or `dev.pathland.view.nativecore`). Renaming is cleaner but requires updating imports in desktop demo and docs. The user suggested `pathland-native-core`, so package `dev.pathland.nativecore` (or `dev.pathland.view.native`) might be better. But AGENTS says the JVM library package conventions are `dev.pathland.view.core.*`, `dev.pathland.view.engine`, `dev.pathland.view.dsl`, etc. A new library could be `dev.pathland.nativecore` or `dev.pathland.view.native`. Let's propose `dev.pathland.view.native` (or `dev.pathland.nativecore`) and note that keeping `dev.pathland.view.core.ffm` is an option for compatibility. Since the desktop demo is the only consumer and it's in-repo, renaming is easy. I'd recommend `dev.pathland.nativecore` to match the artifact `pathland-native-core`. But maybe `dev.pathland.view.native` is more consistent with the `view` family. Hmm.

Let's inspect package naming conventions in lib/java: `dev.pathland.view.core`, `dev.pathland.view.dsl`, `dev.pathland.view.engine`, `dev.pathland.render.html`, `dev.pathland.server`, `dev.pathland.state.redis`, `dev.pathland.quarkus`, `dev.pathland.spring`, `dev.pathland.demo.*`. A new library could be `dev.pathland.view.native` or `dev.pathland.native`. I'd propose `dev.pathland.view.native` (artifact `pathland-native-core`) or `dev.pathland.nativecore`. We can ask the user. But to keep the plan actionable, propose `dev.pathland.nativecore` and note alternative.

- Also the JNA `PathlandCore` class name conflicts with the Rust crate `pathland-core` and the Java `dev.pathland.view.core` package. `PathlandCore` is the JNA binding. In the new module, maybe rename to `NativeCore` or `PathlandCoreNative`. But that's API churn. We can keep `PathlandCore` in the new package. Fine.

- The new module's POM:
```
<parent> pathland-parent </parent>
<artifactId>pathland-native-core</artifactId>
<dependencies>
  <dependency>dev.pathland:pathland-view-core</dependency>
  <dependency>net.java.dev.jna:jna</dependency>
  <dependency>kotlin-stdlib</dependency>
  <test>junit-jupiter</test>
</dependencies>
<build> kotlin-maven-plugin compile/test-compile </build>
<profiles> release -> Dokka javadoc </profiles>
```
- Add `<module>pathland-native-core</module>` to `lib/java/pom.xml` base modules (or demos). If base, it's built in `mvn install` and included in release. The release profile's `maven-source-plugin` etc. apply.
- Add dependency to `pathland-desktop-demo/pom.xml`.
- Remove JNA from `pathland-view-core/pom.xml`.
- Move the two Kotlin files. Since they use `dev.pathland.view.core.*` imports, the new module depends on view-core. No circular dependency.
- The desktop demo also uses JNA directly (`GtkRendererNative`, `QtRendererNative`, `GtkHost`, `QtHost`, `RingEventReader`) so it keeps JNA.
- `pathland-view-core` no longer needs JNA. This removes JNA from the Quarkus/Spring/server classpath entirely, solving native risk.
- Does `pathland-view-core`'s `status.md` mention `JNA` in the description; update. `lib/java/pom.xml` description line 16 and comment line 63 mention JNA ring interop in view-core; update to mention the new module.
- `AGENTS.md` line 145 (view-core package list `.ffm`), line 151 (JNA ring interop), line 129 (`pathland-core-capi` consumed by Kotlin DSL via JNA `dev.pathland.view.core.ffm`), line 272 (Kotlin DSL binds with JNA), line 285 (desktop demo). Update.
- `pathland-desktop-demo/status.md` references. Update.
- Maybe `docs/NLNET-APPLICATION.md` line 65 says "cross-language interop uses JNA" — still true, no change. `docs/GRANT.md` line 66 — still true.
- `scripts/lib.sh` or run scripts build the Rust dylib and set `java.library.path`; they don't reference the Java module. Check. Not needed.
- `pathland-native-core` needs `pathland-view-core`'s protocol constants, which are public. Fine.

Now, base.css:
- Option 1: Keep as-is and add `NativeImageResourceBuildItem` in `pathland-quarkus-deployment`:
  ```
  @BuildStep
  NativeImageResourceBuildItem nativeResources() {
      return new NativeImageResourceBuildItem(
          "dev/pathland/render/html/base.css",
          "dev/pathland/render/html/base.css.name");
  }
  ```
  But `NativeImageResourceBuildItem` is in `io.quarkus.deployment.builditem.nativeimage`; the deployment module already depends on `quarkus-core-deployment`. This registers the resources for any Quarkus app using the extension, no app config needed. This is the cleanest.
  However, is `base.css` on the classpath at build time? Yes, `pathland-render-html` copies it to its `target/classes`, and the deployment module can register the resource path. The native image build then includes it.
  This avoids moving the file and avoids app-specific config.
- Option 2: Move base.css to `lib/java/pathland-render-html/src/main/resources/dev/pathland/render/html/`. But then the canonical source is duplicated from `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html/assets`. The Maven copy step would no longer be needed. But `scripts/sync-design-css.sh` currently syncs `design/build` → `lib/rust/.../assets`. To keep the Java copy in sync, update the script to also copy to `lib/java/.../resources`, or have the Maven build copy. That's more complexity and drift risk. Not recommended.
- Option 3: Move base.css under `META-INF/resources` in `pathland-render-html`. It would auto-include, but expose it as a static web resource at `/META-INF/resources/...`? Quarkus serves `META-INF/resources` at root, so the path would be `/dev/pathland/render/html/base.css` (public). Not desirable, and it changes the classpath resource path used by `BaseCss` (it uses `/dev/pathland/render/html/base.css`). Could use `META-INF/resources/_pathland/...` but then it's public. Not recommended.
- Option 4: Generate a Java class with the CSS string at build time. Overkill.
- Recommendation: Keep base.css where it is; register it via `NativeImageResourceBuildItem` in the Quarkus deployment module. This is better than `quarkus.native.resources.includes` because it's extension-owned and works for all consumers. The user asked "we can move the base.css to resources perhaps?" We should explain it's already a resource in the Java module's output (copied by Maven), and the real issue is native-image registration; the build item solves it without moving/duplicating. If they prefer, we can also add `quarkus.native.resources.includes` in the demo as a belt-and-suspenders, but not necessary.
- Wait: The `pathland-quarkus-deployment` module may not have `pathland-render-html` on its classpath? It depends on `pathland-quarkus` (runtime), which depends on `pathland-server-core`, which depends on `pathland-render-html`. So the resource is on the deployment classpath transitively. `NativeImageResourceBuildItem` just registers a path; it doesn't need the class. Fine.
- But `NativeImageResourceBuildItem` inclusion in native image: The resource must be present in the native-image source jar. Quarkus includes resources registered by build items from the app and dependencies. Good.
- We should also consider the service worker resource `_pathland/sw.js`: it's under `META-INF/resources`, auto-included. The DOM bundle and assets too. Good.
- Do we need `NativeImageResourceBuildItem` for `base.css.name`? Yes, both.
- Is `BaseCss` build-time initialized? If yes, the resources aren't needed at runtime, but registering is harmless and protects against runtime init. Good.

Now, the plan should also include updating `pathland-quarkus/status.md` to mention native resource registration and native support. And `lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo` maybe no status file; add a note to docs/DEPLOY.md.

Now, let's inspect the parent POM release profile and Dokka to plan the new module. Read the rest of lib/java/pom.xml (lines 240+).

# pathland-view-core (JVM engine + DSL) — implementation status

**Last updated:** November 7, 2026

The shared, framework-agnostic JVM engine, runtime and authoring DSL for the
Pathland protocol, written entirely in Kotlin. It owns the `View` SPI and shared
authoring vocabulary, the retained-tree diff emitter,
signals/computed/effects, the wire codec, router, cross-platform state, JNA ring
interop, and the `dev.pathland.view.dsl` SwiftUI-shaped builders/modifiers.
Server and renderer modules depend on this one module; Java hosts consume the
Kotlin-authored views through JVM interop.

## Implemented

- **Protocol** (`dev.pathland.view.core.protocol`): `Components`, `Properties`,
  `Commands` (incl. `SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT`), `Categories`, `ValueTypes`, `Opcode`,
  `ValueEncoder`, `WireValue`, `TokenPath`.
- **Attributed text** (`dev.pathland.view.core.AttributedString`): pure-Kotlin
  model + range-tracking builder (Kotlin char indices → UTF-8 byte offsets) and
  payload encode/decode; `Text(AttributedString)` / `Text(Signal<AttributedString>)`
  emit `SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT` through the emitter and both sinks.
- **Built-in inline Markdown**: `Text("...")` parses the v1 subset by default
  (`**bold**`/`__bold__`, `*italic*`/`_italic_`, `` `code` ``,
  `~~strikethrough~~`, `[label](url)`); `markdown = false` renders literal text.
  `dev.pathland.markdown.Markdown` is now a **pure-Java parser** (no native
  library, so it runs on every platform and under GraalVM native-image); it is a
  behavioural port of the Rust `pathland-markdown` crate (pre-scan + bounded
  cache). The Rust crate remains the parser for the Rust DSL and non-JVM hosts.
  Plain results use the compact `SET_TEXT` path; rich results emit
  `SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT`. Reactive `Text(Signal<String>)` parses on change.
- **Signals** (`dev.pathland.view.core.signal`): `signal`/`state`/`computed`/
  `effect`/`untracked`, synchronous glitch-free flush, equality suppression, error
  caching/retry, circular-dependency detection, and a thread-safe global
  `Scheduler`. `Signals.state` binds to the ambient session `PersistentState`
  during a component render.
- **Topic subscriptions** (`dev.pathland.view.core.subscription`): a strongly
  typed `Topic<T, S>` and the DSL `topic(key, subject, initial)` (also
  `Signals.topic`). Scoped topics name an entity subject; `Topic.global(name)`
  declares an unscoped `Topic<T, GlobalSubject>` with the two-argument
  `topic(key, initial)` form. Both return a normal `Signal<T>` backed by a
  session-local mirror; the server runtime registers it with the app's hub and
  applies published values on the session actor. `SessionContext` (thread-local,
  installed by `PathlandSession` around every actor task) also exposes
  `unsubscribe` and `submit`. Resolution is lazy when a root view's field
  initializer runs before the context is installed.
- **State** (`dev.pathland.view.core.state`): `PersistentState`, untyped
  `StateStore`, in-memory store and provider. Kotlin `Component` state delegates
  bind directly before `body()`; the Java `State` field/binder machinery and
  annotation processor are removed.
- **Transport** (`dev.pathland.view.core.transport`): `ProtocolFrame`,
  `FrameCodec`, `Event`, `EnvironmentData`, `OpcodeSink`, `FrameOpcodeSink`.
  **Hardened (issue #63)**: `FrameCodec.parse` reads the attacker-controlled
  `opcodeCount`/`stringsLen` as unsigned `Long` values and validates them
  against the actual message length before allocating; string offsets are
  bounds-checked (`Parsed.stringAt`). A declared `opcodeCount` that overflows
  `Int` arithmetic now throws instead of triggering an OOM allocation.
- **Router** (`dev.pathland.view.core.router`): `Route`, `RouteTable`, `Router`,
  `Navigation`, `NavigationContainer`, `NavigationIntent`, `Params`, `Chrome`,
  `NavOp`. `NavigationLink` and the navigation helpers live in the Kotlin DSL.
- **JNA interop** (`dev.pathland.view.core.ffm`): lazy `PathlandCore` binding and
  `RingOpcodeSink` over `libpathland_core`.
- **Emitter** (`dev.pathland.view.engine`): `Emitter`, `PathlandNode`, `ViewSlot`,
  `RenderResult`, `InputDispatcher`, `ReactiveValues`, `DateInput`, `MediaInput`.
  Implements mount/id assignment, diff-based reactive emission, node-level binding
  effects, structural reconciliation, fit/media/navigation routing, and the
  zero-opcode unchanged recompute contract. A replaced child is relinked to its
  real parent (not the tree root), so a `SIZE_THAT_FITS` swap cannot detach a
  pinned root `MEDIA_CONTROLLER` or drop its media routing. Registered `MediaController`s are
  projected as pinned, non-visual root children; `unregisterMediaController`
  removes them without touching the app tree.
- **Shared SPI/values** (`dev.pathland.view.core`): `View`, `ViewModifier`,
  `Configurable`, `ChildrenView`, `Modified`, `ViewBuilder`,
  `Environment*`, `Platform`, `Theme*`, `MediaController`, `WindowMetadata`,
  `ProxyConfig`, `Color`, `Length`, shared enums, style protocols, and modifier
  wrappers.
- **Protocol manifest validation** (`ProtocolManifestTest`): the hand-written
  protocol constants (`Components`, `Properties`, `Commands`, `Categories`,
  `ValueTypes`) are checked against `spec/protocol.tsv` — including no extra
  public numeric constants and the full `ValueTypes.forProperty` mapping. No
  Java source is generated.
- **Shared engine traces**: the Kotlin DSL tests run the mount/text/property
  scenarios against the Rust-emitted PLPL fixtures under `spec/engine-traces/`,
  byte-for-byte. The canonical order lives in `spec/ENGINE.md`.
- **Tests**: `pathland-view-core` owns the signal, state, frame-codec, and
  protocol-manifest tests; Kotlin DSL tests exercise the emitter end-to-end, and
  the server/HTML/desktop consumers cover their integration paths.

# pathland-desktop-demo — implementation status

**Last updated:** November 5, 2026

Runs the shared Kotlin `MusicPlayerView` (`dev.pathland.demo.music` from
`pathland-demo-views-kotlin`) under the **native GTK4 renderer**
(`libpathland_gtk`, `dev.pathland.demo.gtk.GtkHost`) or the **Qt Quick renderer**
(`libpathland_qt`, `dev.pathland.demo.qt.QtHost`) — the cross-language,
shared-renderer story. Protocol contract: `spec/`.

## How it works

- The Kotlin DSL mounts the view through its fine-grained `Emitter` into a
  `libpathland_core` shared ring (`RingOpcodeSink`, **zero-copy**).
- The in-process renderer pumps the same ring in place
  (`pathland_gtk_run_ring` / `pathland_qt_run_ring`); no
  `pathland-view-native` host is involved.
- Native inputs round-trip as `EVENT` opcodes that the host drains
  (`pathland_core_drain_events`) and dispatches into the app's bindings via the
  shared `InputDispatcher` (taps, text/value/date inputs, **media events**,
  router back).
- State/theme/platform seeding mirrors the server session: `PersistentState`
  over an `InMemoryStateStore`, `DemoTheme.adaptive()` as the emitter theme.
- **App-driven media**: the renderer plays the demo's tracks and reports
  `MEDIA_*` events back through the ring. The app's web-style
  `/_pathland/assets/...` paths resolve against a local asset root: the demo
  extracts its audio + covers from the shared `pathland-demo-views-kotlin` jar
  at startup (`DemoAssets.extractToTemp`) and calls the renderer's
  `set_asset_root`.

## Implemented

- **`GtkRendererNative`** — JNA binding to `libpathland_gtk`
  (`pathland_gtk_run_ring` + `pathland_gtk_set_asset_root`); library resolved
  from `pathland.gtk.lib` or `java.library.path`.
- **`QtRendererNative`** — JNA binding to `libpathland_qt`
  (`pathland_qt_run_ring` + `pathland_qt_set_asset_root`); library resolved
  from `pathland.qt.lib` or `java.library.path`.
- **`RingEventReader`** (shared, `dev.pathland.demo.desktop`) — decodes raw ring
  `EVENT` opcodes into `dev.pathland.view.core.transport.Event`, resolving
  `TEXT_CHANGED`/`NAVIGATE` strings from the shared host → guest event arena
  (header `0x40`), plus `MEDIA_*` and `FIT_CHANGED` (routed to the emitter's fit
  sink, so the `SizeThatFits` slot swaps to its wide candidate).
- **`GtkHost`** (`main`) — Java host; mounts the Apple Music-style player,
  extracts the demo assets, runs GTK (1180×800), drains and dispatches events.
- **`QtHost`** (`main`) — Kotlin host; mounts the player, extracts the demo
  assets, runs Qt Quick, drains and dispatches events.
- The `Emitter` sets `BINDING_ID` on bound controls for `RingOpcodeSink`s (the
  GTK renderer gates `TEXT_CHANGED`/`VALUE_CHANGED` on it).

## Not implemented / gaps

- **GTK playback requires GStreamer** with the mp3 decoding plugins installed;
  without it the app runs but the pipeline errors on play.
- The GTK renderer's `attach_control_events` covers `TOGGLE`/`SLIDER`/
  `TEXT_FIELD`/`PICKER` only: `DATE_PICKER`, `STEPPER`, `COLOR_PICKER`, and
  `TEXT_EDITOR` render but do not (yet) emit events under GTK.
- Qt6 dev libraries are required to build/run the Qt renderer.
- macOS requires `-XstartOnFirstThread` for both hosts.
- No automated GUI test (headless renderer tests live in the Rust crates).

## Verified by

`mvn test -pl pathland-desktop-demo` — `RingEventReaderTest` (headless, no GTK/Qt;
pointer/value/date/text/navigate/media/fit decoding and bounds behaviour).
Manual: `scripts/run-java-gtk-demo.sh` and `scripts/run-java-qt-demo.sh`.

Now, the new module `pathland-native-core` should probably be a published library? Let's look at the release profile: it publishes all modules in the base reactor. If we add it to the base modules, it will be published. The `demos` profile adds demo modules. The new module is a library, so base modules. It needs Dokka for javadoc. Could copy the view-core profile. Alternatively, if it's only for the desktop demo, add to demos profile and skip publishing. The user's suggestion "Fx. pathland-native-core?" suggests a separate module; likely a library. I'd recommend base modules + Dokka, because native hosts (Java/Swift?) may use it. But note it depends on JNA, which is fine for a native-host library. The server path no longer depends on it.

Now, a subtle issue: `pathland-view-core`'s public API includes `RingOpcodeSink`/`PathlandCore`. Removing them is a breaking change for external consumers. Since this is pre-1.0 (0.2.2), acceptable. But the desktop demo is in-repo. We should note it's a breaking package move. The user wants it, so fine.

Another subtle issue: `pathland-desktop-demo` depends on `pathland-demo-views-kotlin` (which depends on view-core) and directly on JNA. After moving, it needs `pathland-native-core` dependency. The `pathland-native-core` depends on view-core and JNA. The desktop demo's direct JNA dependency is still needed for GtkRendererNative/QtRendererNative/RingEventReader. Could keep it, or rely on transitive JNA from native-core. Better keep direct JNA because it directly uses JNA classes (good Maven hygiene). Fine.

Now, the module's Kotlin compile configuration: copy from view-core. It has only Kotlin sources. Add `kotlin-maven-plugin` compile/test-compile. The test source dir maybe empty; we can omit test-compile if no tests, or add a test to prove the binding resolves? We can move any ffm tests (none). Could add a small test? Not necessary. But for the module to have tests, maybe add a test that `RingOpcodeSink` can be constructed if the native lib is available? That would require the Rust dylib; not in CI. Skip. Keep no test execution or a trivial test. The parent `maven-surefire` will run no tests. Fine.

Now, the `pathland-native-core` module name and package. Let's propose:
- Artifact: `pathland-native-core`
- Package: `dev.pathland.nativecore` (or keep `dev.pathland.view.core.ffm`).
The user wrote "pathland-native-core". I'll propose package `dev.pathland.nativecore` with classes `PathlandCore` and `RingOpcodeSink`, and update the desktop demo imports. If they prefer compatibility, keep the old package. Ask? We can state the recommended option and note the alternative. Since they asked "Fx. pathland-native-core?", likely they want the module name, not necessarily package rename. We can recommend keeping the package `dev.pathland.view.core.ffm` to minimize churn, but then the module name and package mismatch. Hmm. Actually, keeping the package means consumers can switch dependency without code changes; that's a nice migration property. But the package `dev.pathland.view.core.ffm` implies it's part of view-core. The artifact split is the important part. I'd recommend **keep the package** `dev.pathland.view.core.ffm` for source compatibility and to avoid updating imports in desktop demo/docs. The module is just a new artifact containing that package. This is a common pattern (artifact split without package rename). The user can rename later. Let's propose that as the default, with the option to rename to `dev.pathland.nativecore` if they prefer cleanliness. Good.

Now, the base.css question. Let's propose the `NativeImageResourceBuildItem` in `pathland-quarkus-deployment`. Also consider the Spring Boot native? The user only asks Quarkus. But if we register in the Quarkus deployment module, only Quarkus gets it. The `BaseCss` is in `pathland-render-html`, which is also used by Spring. For Spring native, one would need `@NativeHint` or `NativeImageResourcePatterns`. Not asked. We can note. If we move base.css to `src/main/resources` and it's still not under `META-INF/resources`, Spring native still needs registration. So the build-item approach is Quarkus-specific but clean.

Could we instead avoid resources entirely by generating the CSS as a Java string constant? The `BaseCss` class could be generated at build time from the asset file. But that's more work and duplicates. Not needed.

Now, the user asks "we can move the base.css to resources perhaps?"  # Pathland Project - AI Agent Guide
 
 This document provides essential context for AI agents (or human contributors) working on the **Pathland** protocol. It captures the project's direction, architectural decisions, and implementation details to ensure consistency.
 
 **Last Updated**: November 3, 2026
 
 ---
 
 ## Architecture: Rust Opcode Engine
 
 > The canonical core is a **Rust engine** that emits the application's
 > **declarative view structure** — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing, padding,
 > alignment — as a fixed **16-byte opcode ring buffer** into shared linear
 > memory, consumed by host renderers. View components and modifiers are written
 > in Rust with a SwiftUI-like API, and in Kotlin with the hand-written
 > **`dev.pathland.view.dsl` DSL** (reusable JVM library, Java 17+); both drive the
 > engine through the flat **native C ABI** (`pathland-view-native`) over a
 > zero-copy shared ring on desktop. Java hosts mount Kotlin views through
 > `PathlandApp`.
 
 ### The 16-byte Opcode Engine
 
 - Every opcode is exactly **16 bytes**: `Category (1B) | Command ID (1B) | Flags (2B) | A (4B) | B (4B) | C (4B)`, `#[repr(C, packed)]`, little-endian.
 - A 64-byte cache line holds exactly **4 opcodes** → L1-cache-friendly.
 - Opcodes live in a **ring buffer** in linear memory; the guest writes at `writeCursor`, the host reads from `readCursor`; frame boundaries via a monotonic `frameCount` in the header block.
 - **Both directions are binary**: a second **event ring** (host → guest) carries `EVENT`-category opcodes. The renderer writes raw inputs at `eventWriteCursor`; the guest drains them at `eventReadCursor`. Events are 16-byte opcodes through the engine, never a side-channel callback.
 - **Variable-length data** (strings, token paths) lives in a bump **arena**; opcodes reference entries by offset (`[u32 byteLength][bytes...]`), so every opcode stays 16 bytes. A second host-owned **event arena** mirrors this in the host → guest direction (shared-memory event strings, e.g. `TEXT_CHANGED`); over the network, host → guest strings ride the batch's string section.
 - **Window metadata** (`META::SET_WINDOW_METADATA`, field family `TITLE`/`DESCRIPTION`/`LOCALE`) carries the hosting surface's presentation metadata; renderers map it to their own chrome (browser `<title>`/meta description/`<html lang>`, GTK/Qt window title). It is root-scoped and signal-backed, so a route title is a computed over the router. Web-only artifacts (canonical/robots/sitemap) stay host-owned.
 - Spec: **`spec/OPCODE.md`** (primary) + **`spec/CONFORMANCE.md`** (golden vectors). Companion catalogs: **`spec/PRIMITIVES.md`** (views), **`spec/MODIFIERS.md`** (modifiers/properties), **`spec/EVENTS.md`** (events), **`spec/LAYOUT.md`** (frame & layout allocation contract) — draft IDs are allocated there spec-first.
 
 ### Declarative, not positioned (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The engine describes WHAT the UI is — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing,
 > padding, alignment — never WHERE it is. It does not compute layout and does
 > not emit rects.**
 
 - The engine emits **declarative structure** (`TREE` create/delete/insert/remove/move) + **constraint properties** (`PARAMETER` spacing/padding/alignment/FILL/HUG hints).
 - **Native elements everywhere**: each platform's renderer maps the opcode stream onto that platform's native elements — GTK4 widgets on desktop, DOM elements in the browser, HTML server-side — and those native elements lay themselves out. Never a generic canvas unless a platform has no native equivalent.
 - **Reactive emission**: emission is diff-based. Only the nodes that changed emit opcodes (property diffs via `SET_PROPERTY`/`SET_TEXT`, structural diffs via `TREE` opcodes). An unchanged tree emits **zero** opcodes. Signals in the application mark the tree dirty; the engine reconciles.
 - **Zero dynamic heap allocations** during steady-state emission (proven by test).
 
 ### no_std / wasm32 direction guard (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 `pathland-core` and `pathland-view` must remain `#![no_std]` + `alloc` and
 compile for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. This is the guarantee that the protocol
 core can still target a browser / embedded / remote projection later (goal #15,
 Quarkus SSR + WebSocket). The desktop path (`pathland-view-native`) is the only
 consumer today, but the core must not become desktop-only. Verify with
 `lib/rust/check-wasm.sh` (i.e. `cargo build -p pathland-core -p pathland-view
 --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`).
 
 ### Reactive signals (Angular-style)
 
 `pathland-core::signal` provides writable signals that live in the engine. A
 node binds its text (`Node::text_binding`), a property
 (`Node::property_bindings`) or a **string property** (`Node::string_bindings`,
 e.g. a media controller's `MEDIA_SOURCE`) to a `SignalId`; during emit the engine
 resolves the binding and records the dependency, and `Engine::set_signal`
 re-emits **only the bound nodes** (`SET_TEXT` / `SET_PROPERTY`) — no full tree
 walk. Signal values
 are one of `F32`/`U32`/`Bool`/`Enum`/`Str` (packed to the wire's `u32` value or
 arena string). Foreign hosts reach signals via the flat C ABI
 (`pathland_native_signal_create_*` / `signal_set_*` / `node_bind_text` /
 `node_bind_property`) and the Kotlin/JVM `Signal` type. Binding then calling `emit`
 records the dependency; a subsequent `set` is a partial emit. (Computed/derived
 signals + effects are the planned next step.)

 ### HTML base design (`design/`)
 
 The HTML renderer's built-in stylesheet is generated from a **three-layer Style
 Dictionary pipeline** plus hand-authored reset/component CSS (one built-in base
 design; no app-facing base-design selection):
 
 ```
 design/tokens/base/*.tokens.json      # internal palette + scales (not emitted)
 design/tokens/semantic/*.tokens.json  # protocol catalog semantics (emitted)
 design/tokens/component/*.tokens.json # per-component surface (emitted)
 design/html/{reset,components}.css    # hand-authored CSS consuming var(--pl-*)
 design/scripts/{build,dev,check}.mjs  # SD build, watcher/preview, validation
 design/build/base.css                 # generated: reset + tokens + components
 design/build/base.css.name            # content hash: base-<sha256-12>.css
 ```
 
 - Tokens are flat DTCG entries (`$value`/`$type`/`$extensions.pathland`) because
   the catalog has both leaf and group paths (`control.border` vs
   `control.border.width`). Dark values live on `$extensions.pathland.dark`;
   durations/z-index/`em` icon sizes are marked internal.
 - `npm --prefix design run build` generates
   `design/build/{tokens.css,manifest.json,base.css,base.css.name}`;
   `npm --prefix design run check` validates catalog coverage, layer direction,
   dark/forced-dark declarations, dimension/`isLengthToken` rules, and the CSS
   content hash.
 - `scripts/sync-design-css.sh` copies the bundle + name to
   `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html/assets/` (committed; `--check` fails on
   drift). `css.rs` embeds both with `include_str!` (`builtin_css()` /
   `builtin_css_name()`); the Java port copies the same committed assets into
   its jar via Maven resources (`BaseCss`).
 - The renderer's library default is inline (`render_document`); the linked mode
   (`render_document_linked`, C ABI `pathland_html_render_linked` +
   `pathland_html_base_css[_name]`, Java `renderLinked`/`baseCss`/`baseCssName`)
   emits `{base}/base-<hash>.css`. The Spring Boot and Quarkus starters use it
   and serve the renderer-owned bytes immutable (global + mounted bases); token
   overrides/fit rules stay inline.
 - The Maven `refresh-ide` profile and CI run the design build + sync. Do not
   edit generated CSS by hand.
 
 ### Native C-ABI shim (`pathland-view-native` + `pathland-core-capi`)
 
 The **desktop/cross-language zero-copy path**: `pathland-view-native` exposes the
 flat world (the flat `builder`/`engine` surface) as `pathland_native_*` C
 functions with a **shared-memory ring** the host driver reads in place. Any
 language that links the dylib (Swift/Java via FFI) calls the flat surface —
 no per-component wrappers — and consumes opcodes zero-copy.
 
 `pathland-core-capi` (`libpathland_core`) is the **minimal ring C ABI** for the
 Kotlin DSL: `pathland_core_create`/`destroy`, `pathland_ring_buffer_push` (one
 raw 16-byte opcode), `pathland_core_arena_alloc`, frame boundaries, zero-copy
 `ring_ptr`/`ring_len`, and event drain/send. The Kotlin DSL
-(`dev.pathland.view.core.ffm`) binds it with **JNA** (lazily loaded, zero JNI) and
-owns the retained tree + diff emission itself.
+(`dev.pathland.nativecore` in `pathland-native-core`) binds it with **JNA**
+(lazily loaded, zero JNI) and owns the retained tree + diff emission itself.
 
 ### GTK4 Renderer (`pathland-render-gtk`)
 
 The desktop renderer: a single crate that owns **all** GTK/glib/pango usage and
 maps opcode frames **incrementally** onto native GTK widgets (a retained
 `id → gtk::Widget` map). Both the Rust demo and the Java demo render through
 it — the demos **never call GTK or Swing directly**:
 
 - Rust demo links `pathland-render-gtk` as an `rlib` and calls `GtkRenderer::run(...)`
   with a wake closure.
 - The Java/Kotlin desktop demo (`pathland-desktop-demo`) loads `pathland-render-gtk`
   as a `cdylib` via JNA and
   calls `pathland_gtk_run_ring(ring, on_event, width, height)` over the Kotlin view's
   `libpathland_core` ring; native inputs round-trip as `EVENT` opcodes through the shared
   ring. The renderer **writes** the events and **wakes** the host (no payload); the host
   drains the event ring itself via `pathland_core_drain_events`. Events are never
   delivered through a side-channel callback — they flow through the opcode engine.
   The demo mounts the Kotlin `MusicPlayerView` (the same shared view the web demos use) with the
   app-driven media contract: the renderer plays the tracks through a direct GStreamer
   `playbin` and reports `MEDIA_*` events back; the demo's web-style
   `/_pathland/assets/...` paths resolve against an extracted local asset root
   (`pathland_gtk_set_asset_root`).
 
 The renderer maps native inputs onto the raw `Event` surface via GTK4
 controllers (`Button::clicked` → pointer up, `EventControllerMotion` →
 pointer move/enter/leave), emitting events through the same `Pump::send_input`
 path.
 
 `pathland_gtk::run` passes an explicit empty argv to GTK (the process command
 line belongs to the embedding host — e.g. the JVM's `-cp`/`-D` flags — and must
 not be parsed as GTK options).
 
 ### Kotlin JVM authoring DSL (`dev.pathland.view.dsl`, in `lib/java/pathland-view-core`)
 
 The **sole JVM authoring surface**. It is the SwiftUI-like DSL shared by desktop,
 Spring Boot, Quarkus, and web apps. Components and modifiers:
 
 - `View` is an **open Kotlin interface** — the library ships `Text`/`Image`/`Color`/
   `Rectangle`, `VStack`/`HStack`/`ZStack`, `Spacer`, `Button`,
   `TextField(placeholder, WritableSignal<String>)`, `Video` (a
   `MediaController`'s surface), and application code defines its own views by
   extending `Component` or implementing `View`. **Media is a state object, not a
   view** (spec/MEDIA.md): `MediaController` owns the resource + transport as
   signals, a `Video` surface renders it, and **audio has no view** — the app
   binds its own buttons/sliders (`controller.attach()` materializes the
   controller's node once, outside any swapping branch).
 - **SwiftUI-style `body()` / reactive components**: composite views declare
   `View body()`; a signal read there subscribes that component, and a later write
   re-renders only that component and diffs its retained subtree. A signal bound
   to a node stays fine-grained and does not re-run the body. Plain
   `if`/`when`/`for` works; `ForEach` is the reactive list component.
 - **Builders and modifiers**: `VStack(spacing = 8f) { … }`, `Text("hi")`,
   `Button("Save") { … }`, `.padding`, `.frame`, `.fontSize`, `.background`,
   `.buttonStyle(BorderedButtonStyle)`, `.windowMetadata`, navigation intents, and
   the full modifier vocabulary. Styles are Kotlin values
   (`PlainButtonStyle`, `BorderedButtonStyle`, label styles, `NativeVideoStyle`).
 - **Builder scopes**: view blocks take a `PathlandScope` receiver. `PathlandScope`,
   `Navigation.Builder`, and modifier/style `Config` receivers share the
   `@PathlandDsl` marker, so an outer router/config receiver cannot be captured
   implicitly inside a nested view block (compile-time guard only; the
   thread-local `ViewScopes` stack still collects children).
 - **Persisted state**: `Component` provides `val count by state(0)` (auto-keyed
   by property name) or `state(0, "key")`, bound to the session's
   `PersistentState` before the first `body()` render — no annotation processor or
   kapt.
 - **Java hosting**: Java Spring Boot/Quarkus apps remain first-class hosts. A
   Java `PathlandApp` bean returns a Kotlin `View`
   (`return () -> MusicPlayerView.make();`); no Kotlin compiler or authoring DSL is
   needed in the host module. Every reusable Kotlin root exposes a public
   constructor or `@JvmStatic make(...)` factory with Java-friendly types.
 - **Consistency** with `pathland_core::constants` is enforced by the
   emitter/HTML tests (golden byte layout + round-trips).

 ## Project Vision
 
 **Pathland is a cross-platform, cross-language UI protocol** that enables retained-mode UI development with multiple renderer backends. It is **protocol-first**, meaning the protocol specification is the source of truth, not any particular implementation.
 
 **Primary Goal**: Write once, run anywhere - Enable UI code to be written once and deployed across web, mobile, desktop, and embedded platforms through different renderer implementations.
 
 **Status**: The Rust opcode engine (16-byte opcode, ring buffer, arena, diff-based reactive emission) is implemented and tested (`cargo test`). See the Architecture section above.
 
 ---
 
 ## CRITICAL ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLES
 
 ### Principle 1: Renderer Statelessness (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The renderer MUST NOT retain application state.**
 
 - Renderers are **pure functions** of the opcode stream: same opcodes → same output
 - A renderer MAY retain its **rendered-output tree** (id → native element + computed layout) for drawing, hit-testing, and event routing — this is a cache of its own output, not state
 - The renderer MUST NOT retain component property values as business state, application control flow, or anything the application can change without emitting an opcode
 - The application owns the canonical retained UI tree
 - The engine emits **deltas only**; the renderer applies them to its native elements
 
 **Violation of this principle is a bug, not a feature.**
 
 ### Principle 2: Command-Based Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol transmits tree mutations as a stream of commands, NOT as serialized trees.**
 
 - Each frame is a **batch of delta commands** describing changes
 - Only **actual changes** are transmitted (diff-based reactive emission)
 - Protocol acts like a **VM instruction stream** / ABI
 - Deterministic, linear decoding without schema lookup or reflection
 
 ### Principle 3: Binary Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol MUST be binary.**
 
 - Open-source, cross-platform binary format
 - Fixed **16-byte instructions** in a ring buffer shared with the host via linear memory
 - Custom instruction-based bytecode, not schema-driven serialization
 - **Both directions are binary**: tree mutations (app → renderer) AND raw-input events (renderer → app) share the same instruction format, so the wire is language- and platform-agnostic

 ### Opcode Format
 
 Every opcode is exactly 16 bytes:
 
 ```
 [Category: u8][Command: u8][Flags: u16][A: u32][B: u32][C: u32]
 ```
 
 See `spec/OPCODE.md` for the full format, ring buffer, arena, and frame lifecycle.
 
 ### Machine-readable protocol manifest
 
 `spec/protocol.tsv` is the target-neutral ID manifest emitted from
 `pathland_core::constants` by `pathland-protocol-manifest` (`cargo run -p
 pathland-protocol-manifest`). It contains only `kind`, `group`, `name`, and
 `value`; each language binding keeps its own representation and validates or
 reads the manifest. There is no Rust→JVM source generation.
 
 The JVM mirror is hand-written and checked by
 `pathland-view-core/src/test/java/.../ProtocolManifestTest`: every manifest row
 must match a Java constant, no extra public numeric constants may exist, and
 `ValueTypes.forProperty` must match `property_value_type`. CI regenerates the
 manifest from Rust and fails on drift.
 
 Engine behavior beyond individual opcodes is specified in `spec/ENGINE.md` and
 enforced by shared self-contained frame traces under `spec/engine-traces/`.
 `pathland-engine-golden` emits them from the Rust engine and the JVM
 `EngineTraceTest` compares its encoded frames byte-for-byte.
 
 ### Categories
 
 | Category | Value | Direction | Description |
 |----------|-------|-----------|-------------|
 | TREE | 0x01 | Guest → Host | Node create/delete/insert/remove/move |
 | PARAMETER | 0x02 | Guest → Host | Constraint properties (spacing, padding, …), design tokens |
 | EVENT | 0x03 | Host → Guest | Raw inputs: pointer down/move/up, key down/up |
 | META | 0x04 | Both | Reset, environment, window metadata |

 ### Colors
 
 - Literal colors are **sRGB** with D65 white point, packed as `0xAARRGGBB`
 - A color property may instead carry a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference to a token path
 - Semantic token resolution and theme adaptation are **renderer-owned**
 
 ### Design Token System
 
 **Core Principle**: Application defines intent, overrides, and the theme.
 Renderer defines visual appearance, behavior, defaults, and interaction states.
 
 - The **application owns the theme**: token overrides (base = **light**, `dark.`-prefixed = **dark**) and token references in style properties. Token refs cover COLOR and non-color values (`Length` for spacing/padding/font size/radius/border/frame; `FontFamily.Token` for STRING) in the Rust and Kotlin DSLs.
 - The **renderer owns** default token values (light + dark, the full Tier-1 catalog), token resolution (including explicit `dark.` = forced dark and parent fallback), effective color-scheme detection, interaction states (hover, pressed, focus, disabled), and theme adaptation
 - `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` identifies tokens by **dot-separated string paths** (e.g. `color.primary`, `space.2`) with the standard value-type encoding — there is no separate numeric tokenId system. A `dark.` prefix selects the dark variant (`dark.color.primary`); a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference whose path starts with `dark.` forces the dark value in either scheme
 - **Runtime theming**: `META::RESET_THEME` clears every app override; a replacement theme is reset + `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides in one frame. `META::SET_COLOR_SCHEME` forces `platform`/`light`/`dark`. Both are renderer state — no node is re-emitted. Java: `Emitter.replaceTheme`/`setColorScheme` + `PathlandSession.setTheme`/`setColorScheme`; Rust: `Engine::reset_theme`/`set_color_scheme`.
 - An unresolvable token reference leaves the property **unset** (renderer default), never an error or stale value.
 - The protocol MUST NEVER describe hover styles, click styles, visual transitions, conditional styling, or layout tuning for interaction states
 - **Deferred**: applying per-component tokens to native GTK/Qt leaf control chrome; web parent-path fallback.
 
 The HTML renderer's default token values are generated from `design/` (see
 "HTML base design" above). Full details: [Design Token System](./spec/OPCODE.md#design-token-system)
 and the canonical catalog / color-scheme contract in [spec/TOKENS.md](./spec/TOKENS.md).

 ## Implementation Guidelines
 
 ### Adding New Component
 1. Add to `component_type` in `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core/src/constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Implement the component type in `pathland-core` (if it affects the retained tree)
 4. Implement native-element mapping in the target renderer (Goal 3–5)
 5. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Adding New Property
 1. Add to the appropriate property module in `constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Handle the value type in `pathland-core`'s diff emission (if a stack/text/size property)
 4. Implement in each renderer's property application
 5. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Modifying Protocol
 1. Update `spec/OPCODE.md` first (and `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` vectors)
 2. Update `constants.rs` and `pathland-core` encoding/emitters
 3. Run `cd lib/rust && cargo run -p pathland-protocol-manifest` and commit the
    updated `spec/protocol.tsv`
 4. Update the hand-written JVM protocol constants (the Java manifest test fails
    with the exact missing/stale row otherwise)
 5. If emission behavior changed, run
    `cargo run -p pathland-engine-golden -- --emit` and commit the trace fixtures
 6. Verify backward compatibility; update `pathland-core`/renderers + tests
 7. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Changing the Wire Format
 - Bump the wire `version` field in `spec/OPCODE.md` and `pathland-core`'s header (currently 1). Pre-release format changes are acceptable while version stays 1.
 
 ### Keeping implementation status updated (MANDATORY)
 
 **The agent MUST keep the per-project `status.md` files in sync with the code.**
 Whenever you land a protocol or renderer change — a new component/property/
 command/event, a new encoder/decoder, a new widget mapping, a new modifier or
 renderer feature, a test that proves new surface — **update the affected
 project's `status.md`** (Implemented / Not implemented / gaps) in the same
 change. The specs (`spec/`) describe the protocol contract only and MUST NOT
 carry implementation status; status lives in `status.md` next to each
 implementing project.

 ## Common Pitfalls
 
 ### NEVER Do These
 | Anti-Pattern | Why Wrong | Correct |
 |--------------|-----------|---------|
 | Renderer stores application state | Violates statelessness | Application owns the tree |
 | Engine computes layout / emits rects | Violates declarative model | Emit structure + constraints; native elements lay out |
 | Send full trees | Inefficient | Diff-based reactive emission |
 | String property names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
 | String component names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
 | Generic RGB | Ambiguous | Explicitly sRGB |
 | Hover styles in protocol | Renderer job | Define in theme |
 | Heap allocation in steady-state emission | Slow | Preallocated snapshot slab + arena |

 ## Quick Start
 
 1. Read this file, `spec/OPCODE.md`, and `spec/ENGINE.md`
 2. Run Rust tests: `cd lib/rust && cargo test` (runs all crates)
 3. Build/test the JVM libraries: `cd lib/java && mvn install`. The JVM path is
    pure JVM (engine/protocol + HTML renderer + inline-Markdown parser); no Rust
    build is required. Use `mvn -P jvm-only test` for the library/starter subset
    without the demo modules.
 4. Make small changes, verify they work
 
 ---
 
 ## Pathland Mindset
 
 **Always remember**:
 1. Protocol is King
 2. Renderers are Dumb (execute commands only)
 3. Applications are Smart (generate commands)
 4. Only Changes Matter (transmit mutations / reactive emission)
 5. Binary is Beautiful (efficient, deterministic)
 
 **When in doubt**: Check `spec/OPCODE.md`, the conformance vectors in `spec/CONFORMANCE.md`, and the companion catalogs (`spec/PRIMITIVES.md`, `spec/MODIFIERS.md`, `spec/EVENTS.md`, `spec/LAYOUT.md`), and the reference implementation (`pathland-core`). Ask: "Does this maintain stateless renderers?" "Does this only transmit actual changes?" "Does this describe WHAT the UI is, never WHERE?" "Is this representable as a 16-byte opcode in any language?"

 # Security Policy
 
 Pathland is a network-facing binary protocol: the byte decoders and the C ABI
 are security-critical surfaces. This policy covers how vulnerabilities are
 reported and handled.
 
 ## Reporting a vulnerability
 
 **Do not open a public issue for a security vulnerability.** Report it privately
 to the maintainers:
 
 - Email: `michael@apaq.dk`
 - Subject prefix: `[Pathland security]`
 
 Please include:
 
 - The affected crate/module and version (or commit).
 - A description of the vulnerability and its impact.
 - A minimal reproduction (payload bytes or code) where possible.
 - Any suggested fix, if you have one.
 
 We aim to acknowledge reports within **5 business days** and to ship a fix (or a
 mitigation) as soon as a coordinated patch is ready. We will credit reporters in
 the release notes unless anonymity is requested.
 
 ## Scope
 
 The following are in scope for this policy:
 
 - `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core` — the `no_std` protocol core (opcode decode,
   ring buffer, arena, memory layout).
 - `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core-transport` — PLPL batch encode/decode.
 - `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core-capi` — the `unsafe extern "C"` ring ABI
   (`libpathland_core`): pointer-argument handling, zero-copy reads, event drain.
 - `lib/java/pathland-view-core` `transport` — `FrameCodec` (PLPL encode/decode).
 - The `@pathland/dom-renderer` web client (PLPL batch decode + hydration in
-  `lib/typescript/src`, built to `dist/pathland-dom-renderer.js` and copied into
-  both demos).
+  `lib/typescript/src`, built to `dist/pathland-dom-renderer.js` and shipped in
+  the Spring Boot starter + Quarkus extension jars).
 
 Out of scope: dependencies (report those to their respective projects),
 development-only tooling, and the demo application code.
 
 ## Security-sensitive guarantees
 
 - Every 16-byte opcode decoder must **reject malformed/truncated input
   gracefully** (no panics, no out-of-bounds reads, no hangs) — see the hardening
   issues (#37, #38).
 - The C ABI entry points (`pathland_ring_buffer_push`,
   `pathland_core_arena_alloc`, `pathland_core_drain_events`, …) treat
   caller-provided pointers as trusted by contract; the bounds guarantees must be
   upheld and are audited via Miri/sanitizers in CI.
 - No secrets or tokens may ever be committed; see
   [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md).
 
 ## Deployment hardening
 
 Framework- and deployment-level controls (WebSocket origin checks, CSP and
 security headers, transport/message limits, rate limiting, TLS/reverse-proxy
 setup) are documented in [docs/HARDENING.md](./docs/HARDENING.md). The Quarkus
 extension supplies secure defaults; the Spring Boot starter requires the
 `pathland.allowed-origins` property for cross-origin hosts.
 
 ## Security testing
 
 Coverage is tracked by the hardening milestone (issues #37–#39): fuzzing for the
 Rust/TypeScript/Java decoders, Miri + ASan/UBSan on the C ABI, and bounds fixes.
 Results will be linked here as they land.
 
 ## Supported versions
 
 The project is pre-1.0 (`wire protocol version 1`). Security fixes land on the
 default branch and are backported only when a tagged release is actively used;
 see the [Versioning](README.md#versioning) section.
\ No newline at end of file

+[ -z "${MVNW_REPOURL-}" ] || distributionUrl="$MVNW_REPOURL$_MVNW_REPO_PATTERN${distributionUrl#*"$_MVNW_REPO_PATTERN"}"
+distributionUrlName="${distributionUrl##*/}"
+distributionUrlNameMain="${distributionUrlName%.*}"
+distributionUrlNameMain="${distributionUrlNameMain%-bin}"
+MAVEN_USER_HOME="${MAVEN_USER_HOME:-${HOME}/.m2}"
+MAVEN_HOME="${MAVEN_USER_HOME}/wrapper/dists/${distributionUrlNameMain-}/$(hash_string "$distributionUrl")"
+
+exec_maven() {
+  unset MVNW_VERBOSE MVNW_USERNAME MVNW_PASSWORD MVNW_REPOURL || :
+  exec "$MAVEN_HOME/bin/$MVN_CMD" "$@" || die "cannot exec $MAVEN_HOME/bin/$MVN_CMD"
+}
+
+if [ -d "$MAVEN_HOME" ]; then
+  verbose "found existing MAVEN_HOME at $MAVEN_HOME"
+  exec_maven "$@"
+fi
+
+case "${distributionUrl-}" in
+*?-bin.zip | *?maven-mvnd-?*-?*.zip) ;;
+*) die "distributionUrl is not valid, must match *-bin.zip or maven-mvnd-*.zip, but found '${distributionUrl-}'" ;;
+esac
+
+# prepare tmp dir
+if TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR="$(mktemp -d)" && [ -d "$TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR" ]; then
+  clean() { rm -rf -- "$TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR"; }
+  trap clean HUP INT TERM EXIT
+else
+  die "cannot create temp dir"
+fi
+
+mkdir -p -- "${MAVEN_HOME%/*}"
+
+# Download and Install Apache Maven
+verbose "Couldn't find MAVEN_HOME, downloading and installing it ..."
+verbose "Downloading from: $distributionUrl"
+verbose "Downloading to: $TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR/$distributionUrlName"
+
+# select .zip or .tar.gz
+if ! command -v unzip >/dev/null; then
+  distributionUrl="${distributionUrl%.zip}.tar.gz"
+  distributionUrlName="${distributionUrl##*/}"
+fi
+
+# verbose opt
+__MVNW_QUIET_WGET=--quiet __MVNW_QUIET_CURL=--silent __MVNW_QUIET_UNZIP=-q __MVNW_QUIET_TAR=''
+[ "${MVNW_VERBOSE-}" != true ] || __MVNW_QUIET_WGET='' __MVNW_QUIET_CURL='' __MVNW_QUIET_UNZIP='' __MVNW_QUIET_TAR=v
+
+# normalize http auth
+case "${MVNW_PASSWORD:+has-password}" in
+'') MVNW_USERNAME='' MVNW_PASSWORD='' ;;
+has-password) [ -n "${MVNW_USERNAME-}" ] || MVNW_USERNAME='' MVNW_PASSWORD='' ;;
+esac
+
+if [ -z "${MVNW_USERNAME-}" ] && command -v wget >/dev/null; then
+  verbose "Found wget ... using wget"
+  wget ${__MVNW_QUIET_WGET:+"$__MVNW_QUIET_WGET"} "$distributionUrl" -O "$TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR/$distributionUrlName" || die "wget: Failed to fetch $distributionUrl"
+elif [ -z "${MVNW_USERNAME-}" ] && command -v curl >/dev/null; then
+  verbose "Found curl ... using curl"
+  curl ${__MVNW_QUIET_CURL:+"$__MVNW_QUIET_CURL"} -f -L -o "$TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR/$distributionUrlName" "$distributionUrl" || die "curl: Failed to fetch $distributionUrl"
+elif set_java_home; then
+  verbose "Falling back to use Java to download"
+  javaSource="$TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR/Downloader.java"
+  targetZip="$TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR/$distributionUrlName"
+  cat >"$javaSource" <<-END
+	public class Downloader extends java.net.Authenticator
+	{
+	  protected java.net.PasswordAuthentication getPasswordAuthentication()
+	  {
+	    return new java.net.PasswordAuthentication( System.getenv( "MVNW_USERNAME" ), System.getenv( "MVNW_PASSWORD" ).toCharArray() );
+	  }
+	  public static void main( String[] args ) throws Exception
+	  {
+	    setDefault( new Downloader() );
+	    java.nio.file.Files.copy( java.net.URI.create( args[0] ).toURL().openStream(), java.nio.file.Paths.get( args[1] ).toAbsolutePath().normalize() );
+	  }
+	}
+	END
+  # For Cygwin/MinGW, switch paths to Windows format before running javac and java
+  verbose " - Compiling Downloader.java ..."
+  "$(native_path "$JAVACCMD")" "$(native_path "$javaSource")" || die "Failed to compile Downloader.java"
+  verbose " - Running Downloader.java ..."
+  "$(native_path "$JAVACMD")" -cp "$(native_path "$TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR")" Downloader "$distributionUrl" "$(native_path "$targetZip")"
+fi
+
+# If specified, validate the SHA-256 sum of the Maven distribution zip file
+if [ -n "${distributionSha256Sum-}" ]; then
+  distributionSha256Result=false
+  if [ "$MVN_CMD" = mvnd.sh ]; then
+    echo "Checksum validation is not supported for maven-mvnd." >&2
+    echo "Please disable validation by removing 'distributionSha256Sum' from your maven-wrapper.properties." >&2
+    exit 1
+  elif command -v sha256sum >/dev/null; then
+    if echo "$distributionSha256Sum  $TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR/$distributionUrlName" | sha256sum -c - >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+      distributionSha256Result=true
+    fi
+  elif command -v shasum >/dev/null; then
+    if echo "$distributionSha256Sum  $TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR/$distributionUrlName" | shasum -a 256 -c >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+      distributionSha256Result=true
+    fi
+  else
+    echo "Checksum validation was requested but neither 'sha256sum' or 'shasum' are available." >&2
+    echo "Please install either command, or disable validation by removing 'distributionSha256Sum' from your maven-wrapper.properties." >&2
+    exit 1
+  fi
+  if [ $distributionSha256Result = false ]; then
+    echo "Error: Failed to validate Maven distribution SHA-256, your Maven distribution might be compromised." >&2
+    echo "If you updated your Maven version, you need to update the specified distributionSha256Sum property." >&2
+    exit 1
+  fi
+fi
+
+# unzip and move
+if command -v unzip >/dev/null; then
+  unzip ${__MVNW_QUIET_UNZIP:+"$__MVNW_QUIET_UNZIP"} "$TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR/$distributionUrlName" -d "$TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR" || die "failed to unzip"
+else
+  tar xzf${__MVNW_QUIET_TAR:+"$__MVNW_QUIET_TAR"} "$TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR/$distributionUrlName" -C "$TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR" || die "failed to untar"
+fi
+
+# Find the actual extracted directory name (handles snapshots where filename != directory name)
+actualDistributionDir=""
+
+# First try the expected directory name (for regular distributions)
+if [ -d "$TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR/$distributionUrlNameMain" ]; then
+  if [ -f "$TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR/$distributionUrlNameMain/bin/$MVN_CMD" ]; then
+    actualDistributionDir="$distributionUrlNameMain"
+  fi
+fi
+
+# If not found, search for any directory with the Maven executable (for snapshots)
+if [ -z "$actualDistributionDir" ]; then
+  # enable globbing to iterate over items
+  set +f
+  for dir in "$TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR"/*; do
+    if [ -d "$dir" ]; then
+      if [ -f "$dir/bin/$MVN_CMD" ]; then
+        actualDistributionDir="$(basename "$dir")"
+        break
+      fi
+    fi
+  done
+  set -f
+fi
+
+if [ -z "$actualDistributionDir" ]; then
+  verbose "Contents of $TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR:"
+  verbose "$(ls -la "$TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR")"
+  die "Could not find Maven distribution directory in extracted archive"
+fi
+
+verbose "Found extracted Maven distribution directory: $actualDistributionDir"
+printf %s\\n "$distributionUrl" >"$TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR/$actualDistributionDir/mvnw.url"
+mv -- "$TMP_DOWNLOAD_DIR/$actualDistributionDir" "$MAVEN_HOME" || [ -d "$MAVEN_HOME" ] || die "fail to move MAVEN_HOME"
+
+clean || :
+exec_maven "$@"

+++ lib/java/mvnw.cmd	
@@ -0,0 +1,189 @@
+<# : batch portion
+@REM ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
+@REM Licensed to the Apache Software Foundation (ASF) under one
+@REM or more contributor license agreements.  See the NOTICE file
+@REM distributed with this work for additional information
+@REM regarding copyright ownership.  The ASF licenses this file
